content: 1. Labeling for Infectious Substances (Category A): The label for Miscellaneous Dangerous Substances must have minimum dimensions of 100 × 100 mm. For smaller packages, the dimensions can be reduced to 50 × 50 mm. Each package requires one label, and the label must be in black and white. 2. Labeling for Non-Flammable, Non-Toxic Gas: The label for Non-Flammable, Non-Toxic Gas must also have minimum dimensions of 100 × 100 mm, or 50 × 50 mm for smaller packages. Each package requires one label, and the label must be in green and white or green and black. 3. Labeling for Cryogenic Liquids: The label for Cryogenic Liquid must conform to standard A7 dimensions (74 × 105 mm). Each package requires one label, and the label must be in green and white. For air transport involving cryogenic liquids (deeply refrigerated liquefied gases), the label must be affixed to insulated vessels or flasks used as outer packaging. This is in addition to other required labels or marks. 4. Orientation Labels: Orientation labels must have standard A7 dimensions (74 × 105 mm) and must be placed on opposite sides of the package. The label can be in black and white or red and white. The words THIS SIDE UP or THIS END UP may also be displayed on the top cover of the package. 5. Cargo Aircraft Only (CAO) Label: Packages that can only be transported on cargo aircraft must display the Cargo Aircraft Only label. This is particularly relevant for Category A infectious substances (UN 2814 or UN 2900) exceeding 50 ml or 50 grams per package. The label must have minimum dimensions of 120 × 110 mm, or 60 × 55 mm for smaller packages. 6. Documentation Requirements: For air transport, the shipper must prepare and sign a Shipper’s Declaration for Dangerous Goods. A packing list or proforma invoice must include the receiver’s address, the number of packages, details of contents, weight, and value. For international transport, a minimal value must be indicated for customs purposes if the items are supplied free of charge. Import/export permits or declarations may be required. An air waybill or equivalent document must be prepared for air, road, rail, or sea transport. 7. Packaging for Category B Infectious Substances: The triple packaging system is mandatory, even for local surface transport. Testing documents are not required, but the packaging must comply with Packing Instruction P650. For air transport, primary receptacles must not exceed 1 liter for liquids, and the outer packaging must not contain more than 4 liters. For solids, the outer packaging must not exceed 4 kg, except for packages containing body parts, organs, or whole bodies. 8. Refrigerants: Refrigerants such as ice, ice packs, or dry ice must be placed outside the secondary receptacle or in an outer packaging or overpack. Wet ice must be in a leak-proof container, and the outer packaging must also be leak-proof. Dry ice must not be placed inside the primary or secondary receptacle due to the risk of explosion. Packaging must allow the release of carbon dioxide gas if dry ice is used. Liquid nitrogen requires special arrangements with the carrier. Primary receptacles must withstand extremely low temperatures, and the outermost packaging must display the hazard label for liquid nitrogen. 9. Overpacks: Overpacks combine several packages into one unit for transport. When refrigerants are used, overpacks may include insulated vessels or flasks. Required marks and labels on the outer packaging must be repeated on the outermost layer of the overpack. Overpacks must also be marked with the word OVERPACK. 10. Reusing Packaging Materials: Shipping packages can be reused if appropriately disinfected. All marks and labels must reflect the actual substances being shipped. For empty packages, all non-applicable marks and labels must be removed or covered. 11. Training Requirements: Personnel involved in the transport of infectious substances must undergo appropriate training. For Category A substances, this includes attending approved courses and passing examinations. For Category B substances, clear instructions on packaging use are considered sufficient training. Employers must maintain records of training and make them available upon request. Training must be supplemented periodically as deemed necessary by competent authorities. 12. Transport Planning: The shipper is responsible for the correct classification, packaging, labeling, and documentation of infectious substances. Efficient transport requires coordination between the sender, carrier, and receiver to ensure safe and timely delivery. Carriers are not legally obligated to transport specific goods and may refuse to carry certain items. 13. United Nations System: The guidelines align with the United Nations system for the transport of infectious substances. WHO encourages all countries to adopt this system but acknowledges that national or local requirements may take precedence.
